purpose: Public-health background for outbreak alert emails. Every statement is a short paraphrase of the cited public source and lists the source ids it comes from. General information only, not individual medical advice.
translationNote: Facts are kept in English as written from the cited sources; Sinhala and Tamil emails show them in English with a note, pending a reviewed translation.

cdc-lepto.publisher: US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
cdc-lepto.title: About Leptospirosis

whatItIs.text: A viral infection caused by the dengue virus, carried mainly by Aedes aegypti mosquitoes.

howItSpreads.text: Spread by the bite of an infected female mosquito; mosquitoes pick up the virus by biting infected people, including people without symptoms.
An infected mosquito can pass on the virus for the rest of its life.

symptoms.text: Many people have mild or no symptoms and recover in 1 to 2 weeks.
Symptoms usually start 4 to 10 days after infection and last 2 to 7 days: high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, nausea, vomiting, swollen glands and rash.

dangerSigns.text: Severe symptoms often come after the fever goes down: severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, rapid breathing, bleeding gums or nose, blood in vomit or stool, restlessness, extreme thirst, pale or cold skin, weakness.
Anyone with these signs should get medical care immediately.

prevention.text: Avoid bites, especially in the daytime: clothing that covers the body, mosquito nets, window screens and repellents containing DEET, picaridin or IR3535.
Stop mosquito breeding: remove containers that hold standing water, dispose of waste properly, and cover, empty and clean water storage every week.

clinicianNote.text: There is no specific treatment; care is supportive (rest, fluids, paracetamol). NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and aspirin are avoided because they can increase bleeding risk.
Laboratory confirmation uses nucleic acid amplification tests, ELISA or rapid tests; direct detection methods are most useful in the first week of illness.

whatItIs.text: A bacterial disease caused by Leptospira that affects people and many kinds of animals.

howItSpreads.text: Infected animals pass the bacteria in urine, which can contaminate water or soil for weeks to months; people are infected through contact with that water or soil or with animal body fluids.
Risk rises after floods and heavy rain; spread from person to person is rare.

symptoms.text: Fever, muscle aches, headache, nausea or vomiting, jaundice, diarrhoea, chills, stomach pain, red eyes or rash; some people have no symptoms.
Illness usually starts 2 to 30 days after exposure and may come in two phases, the second sometimes more severe.

dangerSigns.text: Without treatment it can cause kidney or liver damage, meningitis, breathing problems and death.
Anyone who may have been exposed and becomes ill should see a healthcare provider right away.

prevention.text: Avoid swimming or wading in water that may be contaminated, especially after floods or heavy rain.
Cover cuts with waterproof dressings and wear waterproof clothing and boots near water or soil that may be contaminated.

clinicianNote.text: Treated with antibiotics such as doxycycline or penicillin, ideally started early; severe illness may need intravenous antibiotics.

whatItIs.text: A life-threatening infection caused by the bacterium Salmonella Typhi, which lives only in humans.

howItSpreads.text: Usually spread through contaminated food or water.

symptoms.text: Prolonged high fever, tiredness, headache, nausea, stomach pain, and constipation or diarrhoea; some people get a rash.

dangerSigns.text: Severe cases can lead to serious complications or death.

prevention.text: Safe water, adequate sanitation and hygiene among food handlers prevent spread; a typhoid conjugate vaccine is available.
Eat thoroughly cooked hot food, boil or disinfect uncertain drinking water, wash hands often, and wash or peel raw produce.

clinicianNote.text: Infection is confirmed by blood testing. It is treated with antibiotics, but antibiotic resistance is common.
People can keep shedding bacteria after symptoms end; a follow-up test is advised to confirm clearance.

whatItIs.text: Three or more loose or liquid stools a day (or more often than normal for the person), usually a sign of an intestinal infection.

howItSpreads.text: Bacteria, viruses or parasites spread through contaminated food or drinking water, or from person to person when hygiene is poor.

symptoms.text: Frequent loose stools with loss of body fluids; vomiting can also occur.

dangerSigns.text: The main danger is dehydration: lethargy or unconsciousness, sunken eyes, drinking poorly or being unable to drink, and skin that returns very slowly when pinched are signs of severe dehydration.
Get care from a health worker for diarrhoea that persists, blood in the stool or any sign of dehydration.

prevention.text: Safe drinking water, improved sanitation, handwashing with soap, good food hygiene, exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months and rotavirus vaccination.

clinicianNote.text: Oral rehydration solution replaces lost fluids; zinc supplements for 10 to 14 days shorten episodes; severe dehydration needs intravenous fluids.

whatItIs.text: An acute respiratory infection caused by influenza viruses; types A and B cause seasonal epidemics.

howItSpreads.text: Spreads easily through droplets from coughs and sneezes and through contaminated hands; in tropical regions it can occur all year.

symptoms.text: Sudden fever, usually dry cough, headache, muscle and joint pain, severe tiredness, sore throat and runny nose, starting about 2 days (1 to 4 days) after infection.
Most people recover within a week; the cough can last two weeks or more.

dangerSigns.text: Complications can include pneumonia and sepsis; severe illness is concentrated in pregnant women, children under 5, older adults and people with chronic conditions or weak immunity.

prevention.text: Yearly vaccination is the most effective prevention.
Wash hands often, cover coughs and sneezes, stay home when ill and avoid close contact with sick people.

clinicianNote.text: Laboratory confirmation (RT-PCR, antigen detection) is needed because other respiratory viruses cause similar illness; rapid tests are less sensitive than RT-PCR.
Antivirals should start as soon as possible for people with severe illness or at high risk.
